mainTopic: Openings (פתח) for releasing vows that we do not use, and the dangers of anger
overview: This עמוד continues the גמרא's discussion of a פתח, an opening that shows a person he would never have vowed had he known something, so a חכם can release the vow. It finishes the story of a mother whose vow made her daughter look bad. Then it tells how רבי ינאי סבא released his grandson's vow by reminding him that a vow makes Heaven examine a person's deeds. The גמרא rules that we do not use that opening, nor several others: רבן גמליאל's פסוק comparing a vower to one who deserves the sword, רבי נתן's teaching that a vow is like building a בָּמָה, and שמואל's statement that a vower is called a רשע. רבי אבהו and רב יוסף bring a פסוק and a משנה to support שמואל. The word רוגז in that פסוק leads to a teaching about how anger brings גיהנם and painful illness. Finally, the גמרא tells a story of a murder on עולא's trip to ארץ ישראל, and רבי יוחנן wonders how such rage could happen there; עולא's answer continues on the next עמוד.

steps.title: The mother's vow is released
steps.stepSummary: The חכם finishes his opening question to the mother: people will assume she vowed because her daughter behaved badly. She says she would not have vowed, so he releases the vow.
steps.simpleTranslation: People would say: 'If her mother hadn't seen bad behavior in her, she wouldn't have made a vow about her for no reason!' Knowing that, would you have made the vow? She said: No. And he released it for her.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes a story that began just before this section. The חכם shows the mother that her vow would make the neighbors suspect her daughter, and she admits she would not have vowed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is a classic פתח: the חכם points to a result the person did not think about when vowing. Once the mother says 'had I known, I would not have vowed,' the vow counts as a mistake from the start, and he can release it.

keyTerms.meaning: Behavior that should be stopped or abandoned; bad conduct
For nothing; for no reason
She made a vow about her
He released it (the vow) for her

phrases.english: If her mother had not seen in her
improper matters that should be stopped,
phrases.notes: This is what the neighbors would say. The חכם is quoting the gossip back to the mother.

phrases.english: she would not have made a vow about her for nothing!
Would you have made the vow about her?
She said to him: No,
and he released it for her.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִילּוּ לָא חֲמָאת בָּהּ אִימַּהּ מִילִּין דַּעֲזִיבָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes a story of a פתח that began before this section.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Showing a vower an unexpected result of the vow, such as harm to someone's reputation, is a valid פתח for release.

steps.title: רבי ינאי releases his grandson's vow
steps.stepSummary: רבי ינאי סבא asks his grandson whether he would have vowed had he known that vowing makes Heaven open his record and examine his deeds. The grandson says no, and the vow is released.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי ינאי סבא's grandson came before him. He said: Had you known that they open your record book in Heaven and look closely at your deeds, would you have vowed? He said: No. And he released it for him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a second story of a פתח. This time the opening is a spiritual one: making a vow causes Heaven to check a person's actions.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Unlike the first story, the 'unexpected result' here is not social. It is a heavenly result: a vow puts your deeds under review. The grandson regrets the vow because of this, so רבי ינאי releases it.

keyTerms.meaning: His daughter's son; his grandson
The Elder
Your record book, your ledger in Heaven
They examine closely (literally, they feel through)

phrases.english: The son of the daughter of Rabbi Yannai the Elder
came before Rabbi Yannai the Elder.
He said to him: Had you known
that they open your record book
and examine your deeds,
would you have vowed?
He said to him: No. And he released it for him.

steps.triggerLanguage: בַּר בְּרַתֵּיה דְּרַבִּי יַנַּאי סָבָא אֲתָא לְקַמֵּיהּ דְּרַבִּי יַנַּאי סָבָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second example of a פתח, this time based on heavenly judgment.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי ינאי used the idea that vowing causes one's deeds to be examined as a פתח to release a vow.

steps.title: The verse behind רבי ינאי's opening
steps.stepSummary: רבי אבא gives the פסוק showing that a vow brings an examination: 'And after vows, to make inquiry.'
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אבא said: Which verse teaches this? 'And after vows, to make inquiry.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אבא asks where the idea in רבי ינאי's story comes from, and he answers with a פסוק from משלי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The idea that a vow 'opens your record book' is not just a scare tactic. It rests on a פסוק: after a person vows, there is an inquiry, meaning his deeds are reviewed in Heaven.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the verse? (Where is this taught?)
To inquire, to examine
Vows

phrases.english: Rabbi Abba said: What is the verse?
"And after vows, to make inquiry."
phrases.notes: משלי 20:25

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the scriptural basis for the idea רבי ינאי used.
steps.raayaObject: The idea that making a vow causes one's deeds to be examined in Heaven.

steps.title: We do not use רבי ינאי's opening
steps.stepSummary: Even though רבי ינאי used this opening, the גמרא rules that we do not open a release this way.
steps.simpleTranslation: And even though רבי ינאי opened for him this way, we do not open with this.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא turns from the story to practical halacha. It says this opening worked for רבי ינאי, but it is not used today.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The step separates what a great חכם once did from what we do in practice. The גמרא does not spell out the reason here. A common explanation is that a person who hears this question may feel pressured or embarrassed and say 'no' without truly regretting the vow.

keyTerms.meaning: And even though
We open (we offer a פתח for release)
We (in our practice)
With this (way)

steps.confusionAlert: Do not think רבי ינאי's release was invalid. The גמרא is not saying he was wrong; it is saying we do not use that opening in our practice.
steps.whyThisMatters: It teaches that not every opening that once worked is a proper פתח for regular practice.

phrases.aramaic: וְאַף עַל גַּב דִּפְתַח רַבִּי יַנַּאי לֵיהּ
phrases.english: And even though Rabbi Yannai opened for him this way,
we do not open for a person with this.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאַף עַל גַּב דִּפְתַח רַבִּי יַנַּאי לֵיהּ אֲנַן לָא פָּתְחִינַן לֵיהּ בְּהָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Limits the practical use of the opening from רבי ינאי's story.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: We do not offer a פתח based on Heaven examining a person's deeds.

steps.title: Another opening we also do not use: רבן גמליאל's verse
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא adds a second opening we do not use. רבי יוחנן reports that רבן גמליאל released an old man's vow by quoting a פסוק about rash speech being like a sword while the tongue of the wise heals.
steps.simpleTranslation: And we also do not open with this other one. As רבה בר בר חנה said in the name of רבי יוחנן: What opening did רבן גמליאל give that old man? 'There is one who speaks rashly like the stabbing of a sword, but the tongue of the wise is healing.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא names a second opening that is not used in practice. It brings רבי יוחנן's report of how רבן גמליאל opened a release for an old man by quoting a פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The format is the same as the last step: a great חכם once used this opening, but we do not. Here the opening is a פסוק from משלי, which the next step will explain.

keyTerms.meaning: Another (other) one
One who speaks rashly; one who utters
Stabbings, piercings
Healing

phrases.english: And we do not open with this other one either,

phrases.aramaic: דְּאָמַר רַבָּה בַּר בַּר חָנָה אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן:
phrases.english: as Rabba bar bar Chana said that Rabbi Yochanan said:

phrases.aramaic: מַאי פְּתַח לֵיהּ רַבָּן גַּמְלִיאֵל לְהָהוּא סָבָא:
phrases.english: What opening did Rabban Gamliel give that old man?
phrases.notes: The old man had made a vow and came to רבן גמליאל to have it released.

phrases.english: "There is one who speaks rashly like the stabbing of a sword,
phrases.notes: משלי 12:18

phrases.english: but the tongue of the wise is healing."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a second opening, parallel to רבי ינאי's, that is also not used in practice.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: We do not offer a פתח using רבן גמליאל's פסוק about rash speech.

steps.title: How רבן גמליאל read the verse
steps.stepSummary: The פסוק is explained: anyone who utters a vow deserves to be stabbed with a sword, but the tongue of the wise, meaning the חכמים who release vows, heals him.
steps.simpleTranslation: Anyone who utters a vow deserves to be stabbed with a sword. But the tongue of the wise heals: the חכמים can release him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains how the פסוק worked as an opening. It shows the vower how serious his vow was and offers the חכמים as his cure.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The 'one who speaks rashly' is the person who makes a vow, and the sword shows how serious that is. The 'tongue of the wise' is the חכם who can undo the vow. Hearing this, the old man regretted his vow, but this is still an opening we do not use in practice.

keyTerms.meaning: Deserving, fit
To stab him, to pierce him
But rather

steps.whatToRemember: A פתח shows that the person would never have vowed had he known something. The גמרא lists two openings once used by great חכמים, רבי ינאי's (Heaven checks your deeds) and רבן גמליאל's (a vower deserves the sword), and rules that we do not open with either one.

phrases.english: Anyone who utters a vow
deserves to be stabbed with a sword,
but the tongue of the wise is healing.
phrases.notes: In other words, the חכמים can release the vow and save him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the פסוק quoted in the previous step.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The פסוק means a vower deserves the sword, but the חכמים can heal him by releasing the vow.

steps.title: Another opening we do not use: רבי נתן's comparison of a vow to a private altar
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a third opening that is not used: רבי נתן's ברייתא saying a vower is like one who built a בָּמָה, and one who keeps the vow is like one who offers a קרבן on it.
steps.simpleTranslation: We also do not open a release with this other idea, as a ברייתא teaches: רבי נתן says, one who vows is like someone who built a private altar, and one who keeps the vow is like someone who brings an offering on it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds one more opening to the list of openings we do not use. This one is רבי נתן's harsh comparison between vowing and building a forbidden altar.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Like the earlier openings in steps 4 and 5, this idea would make the vower regret his vow. רבי נתן's ברייתא has two parts: making the vow, and keeping the vow. That split sets up the next step, where אביי and רבא argue about each part separately.

keyTerms.meaning: We open, meaning we offer a reason that lets the vower regret his vow so it can be released
Another one, here another opening
A private altar outside the בית המקדש, which is forbidden
One who keeps it, meaning one who fulfills the vow

steps.confusionAlert: This line says we do not use רבי נתן's idea, but the next steps show a debate about it. The opening line is really the final הלכה, stated up front before the debate is laid out.

phrases.english: And we do not open with this other one,
phrases.notes: "Open" here means finding an opening to release the vow, like the openings in the steps before.

phrases.english: as it is taught in a ברייתא: Rabbi Natan says:
One who vows is as if he built a private altar,
and one who keeps it is as if he brings an offering on it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a third opening to the list of openings we do not use, after רבי ינאי's and רבן גמליאל's.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי נתן's comparison of vowing to building a בָּמָה is not used as an opening.

steps.title: First version: the first part may be used, and the second part is debated
steps.stepSummary: In the first version, everyone agrees that the first part (vowing is like building a בָּמָה) may be used as an opening. אביי and רבא argue about the second part (keeping the vow is like offering on it).
steps.simpleTranslation: With the first part, we do open. With the second part, אביי says we open with it, and רבא says we do not.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא splits רבי נתן's ברייתא into its two parts and reports who allows each part as an opening.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Saying 'you built a בָּמָה' only criticizes the act of vowing, and in this version all agree it may be used. Saying 'keeping your vow is like offering on it' criticizes even fulfilling the vow, and here אביי and רבא argue.

keyTerms.meaning: The first part of a teaching
The last part of a teaching
An אמורא who often argues with רבא
An אמורא who often argues with אביי

phrases.english: With the first part, we do open.
phrases.notes: The first part is "one who vows is as if he built a private altar."

phrases.english: With the latter part, Abaye said: we do open,
phrases.notes: The latter part is "one who keeps it is as if he brings an offering on it."

phrases.english: Rava said: we do not open.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Breaks down רבי נתן's ברייתא from step 7 into its two parts and gives the debate over each.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In this version, the רישא may be used; on the סיפא, אביי allows it and רבא does not.

steps.title: Two versions of the debate: רב כהנא and רב טביומי
steps.stepSummary: The version just given was taught by רב כהנא. רב טביומי taught it the other way: all agree the second part is not used, and the argument is over the first part.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב כהנא taught this teaching in the wording just given. רב טביומי taught it this way: with the second part, we do not open. With the first part, אביי says we open, and רבא says we do not.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא reports a second version of the אביי and רבא argument, in which the debate is moved to the first part.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both versions agree that the second part, about keeping the vow, is harsher. They differ only on how far the argument goes. In רב טביומי's version, רבא will not use even the first part, so he would not use רבי נתן's ברייתא at all.

keyTerms.meaning: Teaches or reports a teaching in a certain form
A teaching or discussion of the אמוראים
Wording, or a version of a teaching

phrases.english: Rav Kahana teaches it,
this teaching, in this wording.
phrases.notes: He means the version in the step just before.

phrases.english: Rav Tavyumei teaches it this way:
With the latter part, we do not open.
With the first part, Abaye said: we do open,
Rava said: we do not open.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב כָּהֲנָא מַתְנֵי לַהּ לְהָא שְׁמַעְתָּא בְּהָדֵין לִישָּׁנָא. רַב טַבְיוֹמֵי מַתְנֵי הָכִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a second version of the debate in step 8, moving the argument from the סיפא to the רישא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In רב טביומי's version, all agree the סיפא is not used; on the רישא, אביי allows it and רבא does not.

steps.title: The הלכה: neither part of רבי נתן's ברייתא is used
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rules that neither the first part nor the second part of רבי נתן's ברייתא is used as an opening.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the הלכה is: we do not open with either the first part or the second part.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא settles the debate and gives the final rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This rule matches רבא in רב טביומי's version, the strictest view. It also explains the opening line of step 7: we do not use רבי נתן's teaching at all.

keyTerms.meaning: And the הלכה is, the final practical ruling

steps.whatToRemember: רבי נתן's comparison (vow = בָּמָה, keeping it = offering on it) is never used as an opening to release a vow, neither part of it.

phrases.english: And the halacha is: we do not open
neither with the first part nor with the latter part.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהִלְכְתָא: לָא פָּתְחִינַן לָא בְּרֵישָׁא וְלָא בְּסֵיפָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Decides between the views given in steps 8 and 9.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Neither part of רבי נתן's ברייתא may be used as a פתח.

steps.title: Another opening we do not use: שמואל says a vower is called a רשע
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא adds that שמואל's statement is also not used as an opening: even if a person keeps his vow, he is called a רשע.
steps.simpleTranslation: We also do not open with this teaching of שמואל, for שמואל said: even though he keeps his vow, he is called wicked.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds a fourth opening that we do not use. This one is שמואל's statement that anyone who vows is called a רשע.
steps.deeperAnalysis: שמואל goes further than just criticizing a broken vow. Even a person who keeps his vow is called wicked, simply because he took on a vow. The next two steps bring sources for this idea.

keyTerms.meaning: An early אמורא in בבל
A wicked person
Even though

phrases.english: And we also do not open with this one of Shmuel.
For Shmuel said:

phrases.aramaic: אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁמְּקַיְּימוֹ — נִקְרָא רָשָׁע.
phrases.english: Even though he keeps it, he is called wicked.
phrases.notes: "It" is the vow. He is speaking about a person who made a vow.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְלָא פָּתְחִינַן בְּהָא נָמֵי דִּשְׁמוּאֵל. דְּאָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds another opening to the list of openings we do not use.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: שמואל's statement that one who vows is called a רשע is not used as an opening.

steps.title: רבי אבהו's source for שמואל: the shared word for refraining
steps.stepSummary: רבי אבהו supports שמואל with a גזירה שוה. The word for 'refraining' is used about vows and also about the רשעים in איוב, which links vowing to wickedness.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אבהו said: what is the פסוק? 'And if you refrain from vowing, there will be no sin in you.' He learns 'refraining' from 'refraining.' Here it says 'if you refrain from vowing,' and there it says 'there the wicked refrain from troubling.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אבהו shows where שמואל's idea comes from. He links two פסוקים that share the same word.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both פסוקים use the root חדל, which means to stop or refrain. In איוב that word describes the רשעים. Because the same word appears with vowing, the גמרא learns that a person who does not refrain from vowing is connected to the רשעים.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the פסוק, meaning what is the source
And he learns or derives
Refraining or stopping, the shared word in this גזירה שוה
It is written here, and it is written there: the standard way to set up a גזירה שוה

phrases.english: Rabbi Abahu said: What is the verse?

phrases.aramaic: ״וְכִי תֶחְדַּל לִנְדֹּר לֹא יִהְיֶה בְךָ חֵטְא״,
phrases.english: "And if you refrain from vowing, there will be no sin in you,"
phrases.notes: דברים 23:23

phrases.english: And he learns "refraining" from "refraining."
phrases.notes: The same Hebrew word appears in two פסוקים, so he learns one from the other.

phrases.english: It is written here: "And if you refrain from vowing,"
and it is written there: "There the wicked refrain from troubling."
phrases.notes: איוב 3:17

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Provides the פסוק behind שמואל's statement in step 11.
steps.raayaObject: שמואל's claim that one who vows is called a רשע.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A גזירה שוה on the word חדל, from דברים 23:23 and איוב 3:17.

steps.title: רב יוסף's support from the משנה: 'like the vows of the wicked'
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף shows that a משנה already assumes vowing is the way of the wicked. Saying 'like the vows of the proper people' means nothing, but saying 'like the vows of the wicked' creates a real vow.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יוסף said: we also learned this in a משנה. If someone says 'like the vows of the proper people,' he has said nothing. If he says 'like the vows of the wicked,' he has made a vow of נזיר, of a קרבן, and of a שבועה.
steps.whatsHappening: רב יוסף brings a second support for שמואל, this time from a משנה rather than a פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Proper people do not make vows, so comparing your words to 'their vows' says nothing. 'The vows of the wicked' do exist, so that phrase creates a real vow. This shows the משנה agrees that vowing is the way of רשעים, just as שמואל said.

keyTerms.meaning: We too have learned this, meaning a משנה supports this idea
Proper, upright people
A person who vows to avoid wine and haircuts and to stay away from טומאה of the dead
An oath

steps.whatToRemember: There are four openings we do not use: רבי ינאי's (Heaven examines your deeds), רבן גמליאל's (a vow is like a sword), רבי נתן's (a vow is like a בָּמָה), and שמואל's (a vower is called a רשע). The idea that vowing is the way of רשעים is supported both by a פסוק and by a משנה.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב יוֹסֵף, אַף אֲנַן נָמֵי תְּנֵינָא:
phrases.english: Rav Yosef said: We too have learned this:
phrases.notes: He is quoting a משנה from earlier in this מסכת.

phrases.english: "Like the vows of the proper people": he has said nothing,
"Like the vows of the wicked": he has vowed
to be a nazirite, and to bring an offering, and with an oath.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב יוֹסֵף, אַף אֲנַן נָמֵי תְּנֵינָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a second support for שמואל, from a משנה instead of a פסוק.
steps.raayaObject: שמואל's view that vowing is the way of רשעים.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה in נדרים (ט.) that treats 'the vows of the wicked' as a real vow and 'the vows of the proper people' as meaningless.

steps.title: An angry person is ruled by every kind of גיהנם
steps.stepSummary: רבי שמואל בר נחמני quotes רבי יונתן: anyone who gets angry is ruled by all kinds of גיהנם, learned from פסוקים in קהלת and משלי.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי שמואל בר נחמני said in the name of רבי יונתן: Anyone who gets angry, all kinds of גיהנם rule over him. The פסוק says, 'Remove anger from your heart and put away evil from your flesh.' 'Evil' here means גיהנם, because another פסוק says, 'ה׳ made everything for His purpose, even the wicked for the day of evil.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new teaching about how dangerous anger is. It proves it from two פסוקים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק in קהלת puts 'anger' right next to 'evil,' so getting rid of anger keeps away 'evil.' The פסוק in משלי shows that 'evil' (the 'day of evil' saved for the רשע) means גיהנם. So anger leads to גיהנם.

keyTerms.meaning: A person who gets angry
Gehenna, the place where the wicked are punished
Rule over him, have power over him
Evil, or trouble. Here it is read as meaning גיהנם

phrases.english: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani said
that Rabbi Yonatan said:
Anyone who gets angry,
all kinds of Gehenna rule over him,
as it is stated: "Remove anger from your heart
and put away evil from your flesh,"
phrases.notes: קהלת 11:10

phrases.english: and "evil" means nothing other than Gehenna,
as it is stated: "ה׳ made everything for His purpose,
even the wicked for the day of evil."
phrases.notes: משלי 16:4. The 'day of evil' saved for the wicked is גיהנם.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי שְׁמוּאֵל בַּר נַחְמָנִי אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹנָתָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A side teaching connected to the theme of anger (רוגז) from the פסוק in איוב quoted in step 12.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Anyone who gets angry is ruled by all kinds of גיהנם.

steps.title: Anger also brings a painful illness
steps.stepSummary: רבי יונתן adds that an angry person also suffers from תחתוניות (hemorrhoids), learned from a פסוק in דברים.
steps.simpleTranslation: And not only that, hemorrhoids rule over him too. The verse says, 'ה׳ will give you there a trembling heart, failing eyes, and pain of soul.' What sickness makes the eyes fail and brings pain to the soul? It must be hemorrhoids.
steps.whatsHappening: The same teaching continues. Besides גיהנם, anger also brings a painful body illness in this world.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק starts with 'לב רגז', an angry, trembling heart. It goes on to say this comes with failing eyes and pain of soul. The גמרא asks which illness causes exactly those things and answers that it is תחתוניות.

keyTerms.meaning: And not only that, but also
Hemorrhoids, a painful illness of the lower body
A trembling, angry heart
You must say, it can only be

steps.whatToRemember: Anger has two punishments here: all kinds of גיהנם, and painful illness in this world.

phrases.english: And not only that, but
hemorrhoids rule over him,
phrases.notes: Literally 'the lower ones,' meaning a painful illness of the lower body.

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: ״וְנָתַן ה׳ לְךָ שָׁם לֵב רַגָּז
phrases.english: as it is stated: "ה׳ will give you there a trembling heart
and failing of eyes and pain of soul."
phrases.notes: דברים 28:65. 'רגז' is the word that ties this פסוק to anger.

phrases.english: Which thing is it
that makes the eyes fail
and brings pain to the soul?
You must say: this is hemorrhoids.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְלֹא עוֹד אֶלָּא שֶׁהַתַּחְתּוֹנִיּוֹת שׁוֹלְטוֹת בּוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a second punishment for anger to רבי יונתן's teaching.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An angry person also suffers from תחתוניות.

steps.title: A murder on עולא's journey
steps.stepSummary: On his way to ארץ ישראל, עולא travels with two men. One kills the other and asks עולא if he did right. עולא says yes and even tells him to open the cut wider.
steps.simpleTranslation: When עולא was going up to ארץ ישראל, two men from חוזאי joined him. One got up and slaughtered his friend. He asked עולא, 'Did I do right?' עולא answered, 'Yes, and open up the cut.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a story that shows how terrible anger can get. It also sets up the questions that come next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: One traveler kills the other in a fit of rage. עולא agrees with him and even tells him to finish the job, so the victim dies faster. The next steps ask whether עולא acted properly.

keyTerms.meaning: An אמורא who often traveled between בבל and ארץ ישראל
He slaughtered him, cut his throat
Did I do right?
The place of the cut

phrases.english: Ulla, when he went up to Eretz Yisrael,

phrases.aramaic: אִיתְלְווֹ לֵיהּ תְּרֵין בְּנֵי חוֹזָאֵי בַּהֲדֵיהּ.
phrases.english: two men from Chozai joined him.
One got up and slaughtered his friend.
He said to Ulla:
Did I do right?
He said to him: Yes,
and open up the cut.
phrases.notes: He means: finish the job, so the man dies quicker.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A story showing how far anger can go, following the teaching about anger.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Story: an angry traveler kills his companion, and עולא agrees with him out loud.

steps.title: עולא worries he encouraged a sinner
steps.stepSummary: עולא comes to רבי יוחנן and asks if he did wrong by supporting the murderer.
steps.simpleTranslation: When עולא came before רבי יוחנן, he said to him: Maybe, Heaven forbid, I strengthened the hands of sinners?
steps.whatsHappening: עולא asks רבי יוחנן whether what he said to the killer was a sin. The answer comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Praising a sinner can encourage him, and that is wrong. עולא is afraid that by saying 'yes' he supported a murderer.

keyTerms.meaning: Heaven forbid
I strengthened the hands of, I encouraged
Sinners, people doing a sin

phrases.english: When he came before Rabbi Yochanan,
he said to him:
Maybe, Heaven forbid,
I strengthened the hands of sinners?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: עולא questions whether his reply in the story was allowed.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Was עולא wrong to agree with the murderer?

steps.title: You saved your life
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן answers that עולא did nothing wrong. He said it to save his own life.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: You saved your life.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן tells עולא that his words were allowed, because he said them to save himself.
steps.deeperAnalysis: עולא was traveling with an angry killer and could have been the next victim. Saying 'yes' was a way to stay alive, so it is not counted as supporting a sinner.

keyTerms.meaning: You saved your life

phrases.english: He said to him: You saved your life.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers עולא's question.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: עולא acted properly, since he spoke to save his own life.

steps.title: How could such anger happen in ארץ ישראל?
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן wonders: the פסוק about a 'trembling, angry heart' speaks about exile in בבל. So how could someone get this angry in ארץ ישראל?
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן wondered: The verse says, 'ה׳ will give you there a trembling heart.' Isn't that written about Babylonia?
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן is puzzled by the story itself. A rage that leads to murder belongs to exile, so how did it happen on the way to ארץ ישראל?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word 'there' in the פסוק points to exile. That suggests an angry heart is a curse of living in בבל, not of ארץ ישראל. The story seems to go against this.

keyTerms.meaning: He was wondering, he was surprised
Now, after all
Babylonia, the land of exile

phrases.english: Rabbi Yochanan was wondering:
Now, it is written:
"ה׳ will give you there a trembling heart"
Isn't that written about Babylonia?
phrases.notes: 'There' in the פסוק means in exile, so the angry heart belongs to exile, not ארץ ישראל.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to the story and questions how it fits the פסוק from step 15.
steps.kashyaTarget: The story of the murder in ארץ ישראל
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The פסוק places the 'angry heart' in exile, so murderous rage should not happen in ארץ ישראל.

steps.title: עולא begins his answer
steps.stepSummary: עולא starts to answer: 'At that time...' The rest of his answer continues in the next part of the גמרא.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: At that time...
steps.whatsHappening: עולא begins to answer רבי יוחנן's question. The sentence is finished on the next עמוד.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words 'at that time' show that the answer will depend on when and where the murder happened. The full explanation comes right after.

keyTerms.meaning: At that time

phrases.english: He said to him: At that time

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts the answer to רבי יוחנן's question.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Clarifying the time of the event (continues next)
steps.terutzMaskana: The answer depends on when the event took place. The details follow in the next section.
